title: Covalent Bonding
lead: Atoms that attract electrons about equally do not transfer them but share them, and a shared pair of electrons held by both nuclei is a covalent bond. The energy of two approaching hydrogen atoms gives the bond length. Electronegativity is the tendency of a bonded atom to draw the shared electrons toward itself, and the difference in electronegativity between two atoms decides whether a bond is pure covalent, polar covalent or ionic.
objectives: Describe the formation of covalent bonds
Define electronegativity and assess the polarity of covalent bonds
summary_html: Covalent bonds form when electrons are shared between atoms and are attracted by the nuclei of both atoms. In pure covalent bonds, the electrons are shared equally. In polar covalent bonds, the electrons are shared unequally, as one atom exerts a stronger force of attraction on the electrons than the other. The ability of an atom to attract a pair of electrons in a chemical bond is called its electronegativity. The difference in electronegativity between two atoms determines how polar a bond will be. In a diatomic molecule with two identical atoms, there is no difference in electronegativity, so the bond is nonpolar or pure covalent. When the electronegativity difference is very large, as is the case between metals and nonmetals, the bonding is characterized as ionic.

figures.original_caption: The potential energy of two separate hydrogen atoms (right) decreases as they approach each other, and the single electrons on each atom are shared to form a covalent bond. The bond length is the internuclear distance at which the lowest potential energy is achieved.
The electronegativity values derived by Pauling follow predictable periodic trends, with the higher electronegativities toward the upper right of the periodic table.

exercises.prompt: Silicones are polymeric compounds containing, among others, the following types of covalent bonds: Si–O, Si–C, C–H, and C–C. Using the electronegativity values in Figure 7.6, arrange the bonds in order of increasing polarity and designate the positive and negative atoms using the symbols δ+ and δ–.
What information can you use to predict whether a bond between two atoms is covalent or ionic?

answer.solution: The section offers two guides, and it says which one is the better. Look first at the electronegativity difference between the two atoms, read from Figure 7.6 and placed on the scale of Figure 7.8, and then at the kinds of atoms involved and where they sit in the periodic table, remembering the exceptions the section lists for HF, NH<sub>3</sub>, NaCl and MnI<sub>2</sub>.

Explain the difference between a nonpolar covalent bond, a polar covalent bond, and an ionic bond.

answer.solution: Think about what happens to the bonding electrons in each case. The passage on pure and polar covalent bonds describes how the shared electrons are distributed when the two atoms are identical and when they are different, and the passage on bond type describes the range from electrons shared completely equally to electrons not shared at all. Figure 7.8 ties each of the three bond types to a range of electronegativity difference.

exercises.prompt:
From its position in the periodic table, determine which atom in each pair is more electronegative:
(a) Br or Cl
(b) N or O
(c) S or O
(d) P or S
(e) Si or N
(f) Ba or P
(g) N or K

answer.solution: (a) Cl; (b) O; (c) O; (d) S; (e) N; (f) P; (g) N

exercises.prompt:
From its position in the periodic table, determine which atom in each pair is more electronegative:
(a) N or P
(b) N or Ge
(c) S or F
(d) Cl or S
(e) H or C
(f) Se or P
(g) C or Si

answer.solution: Use the two trends the section states: electronegativity increases from left to right across a period and decreases down a group. For a pair in the same group, the atom higher up is the more electronegative; for a pair in the same period, the atom farther to the right. Where the two atoms differ in both row and column, as in (b) and (f), or where one is hydrogen, as in (e), check your prediction against the values in Figure 7.6.

exercises.prompt:
From their positions in the periodic table, arrange the atoms in each of the following series in order of increasing electronegativity:
(a) C, F, H, N, O
(b) Br, Cl, F, H, I
(c) F, H, O, P, S
(d) Al, H, Na, O, P
(e) Ba, H, N, O, As

answer.solution: (a) H, C, N, O, F; (b) H, I, Br, Cl, F; (c) H, P, S, O, F; (d) Na, Al, H, P, O; (e) Ba, H, As, N, O

exercises.prompt:
From their positions in the periodic table, arrange the atoms in each of the following series in order of increasing electronegativity:
(a) As, H, N, P, Sb
(b) Cl, H, P, S, Si
(c) Br, Cl, Ge, H, Sr
(d) Ca, H, K, N, Si
(e) Cl, Cs, Ge, H, Sr

answer.solution: Place each atom in the periodic table and apply the two trends, rising across a period and falling down a group. Atoms of one group, such as N, P, As and Sb in (a), fall in order down the group, and atoms of one period, such as Si, P, S and Cl in (b), rise in order across it. Hydrogen belongs to neither trend in an obvious way, so place it by its value in Figure 7.6.

Which is the most polar bond?
(a) C–C
(b) C–H
(c) N–H
(d) O–H
(e) Se–H

answer.solution: The polarity of a bond grows with the absolute value of the electronegativity difference between its two atoms, as Example 7.3 shows. Find the difference for each of the five bonds from the values in Figure 7.6, or set each pair on Figure 7.5 + 7.8, and compare them.

exercises.prompt:
Identify the more polar bond in each of the following pairs of bonds:
(a) HF or HCl
(b) NO or CO
(c) SH or OH
(d) PCl or SCl
(e) CH or NH
(f) SO or PO

answer.solution: (a) HF; (b) CO; (c) OH; (d) PCl; (e) NH; (f) PO; (g) CN

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following molecules or ions contain polar bonds?
(a) O3
(b) S8
(c) O22−
(d) NO3−
(e) CO2
(f) H2S
(g) BH4−

answer.solution: A bond between two atoms of the same element is a pure covalent bond, since the two atoms have identical electronegativities, and a bond between atoms of different elements is polar to the extent that their electronegativities differ. So look at which atoms are bonded to which in each formula: a species made of one element only has no polar bond, and for the others compare the electronegativities of the bonded atoms in Figure 7.6.
